choices.term: Ὁ λόγος ἡμῶν ὁ πρὸς ὑμᾶς
choices.why: Paul's preaching (2 Corinthians 1:18), continuing the sentence begun in the previous section; not Christ the Word.
Paul's word from 2 Corinthians 1:20, glossed by Cyril as 'in truth'.
rejected: in the Temple (a misreading as ναός)

choices.english: the learned men ... will hold differing opinions
choices.why: δοξάζω here is 'to hold an opinion', set against the steady truth of the gospel.
θεηγόρος, one who speaks of or for God: the prophets and apostles.

choices.term: καίτοι τοῦ Θεοῦ καὶ Πατρὸς τὰ ἀγαθὰ διανέμοντος
choices.english: though it is God the Father who distributes the good things
choices.why: Genitive absolute: the Father is the subject.

choices.english: every prayer will reach its fulfillment
choices.why: πέρας εὐχῆς, the end or fulfillment of a prayer, which Cyril calls the Amen.
rejected: everything shall be the end of prayer

choices.term: οὐκ ἂν ἀμοιρήσειεν αὐτὸς τοῦ δοξολογεῖσθαι πρέπειν
choices.english: He Himself would not lack the glory that befits Him
choices.why: ἀμοιρέω with a negative: He has His share of fitting glory.
rejected: he would not be thought fitting to be glorified

choices.english: and when the prophet Isaiah says
choices.why: γεμήν is the particle γε μήν, not a form of γέμω.
rejected: the fullness of the prophet Isaiah

pass_a_gloss: [opens mid-sentence; the prior section ends 'that his word had not become double and'] obscure (ἀσαφής) the word (λόγος), but rather simple (ἁπλοῦς) and true (ἀληθής), he assures (πληροφορέω) [col. 323], saying 'Our word to you did not become yes and no'; that is, not himself fighting (μάχομαι) with himself and having been sick (νοσέω, pf.) with inconsistency (τὸ ἀσύμβατον), at one time praising (ἐπαινέω) this, at another blaming (ψέγω), but speaking truth (ἀληθεύω) in the preaching (κήρυγμα); faithful (πιστός) then is God, that is, without lie (ἀψευδής) and true. Of the Greeks the picked men (λογάς) about the gods supposed (ὑπολαμβάνω, pf. pass.) among them will hold opinions (δοξάζω, fut.) differently (διαφόρως), saying yes and no; for not among them is the truth but rather the lie (ψεῦδος); therefore also by differing opinions (δόξα) they are shaken (σαλεύω, pass.); but the one truly and by nature Son of the God who is able for all things (πάντα ἰσχύω), how could he become yes and no? [a row of dots in the print marks a gap] Necessarily then also the Son by nature from him, the one proclaimed (κηρύσσω, aor. pass.) among you through us, through me and Silvanus and Timothy, did not become yes and no; for every word about him has become true through the voice (φωνή) of those who speak for God (θεηγόρος). And as many, he says, as [are] promises (ἐπαγγελία) of God, in him the yes; that is, every bounty (φιλοτιμία) and promise (ὑπόσχεσις) we have had (ἔχω, pf.) in him from the God and Father; and this in the Yes, that is, in truth; for these things have come (ἥκω) to an end (πέρας) through Christ; 'for death was swallowed (καταπίνω, aor. pass.) into victory (νῖκος)', and the might (κράτος) of corruption (φθορά) was shaken down (κατασείω, aor. pass.), and the feebleness (τὸ ἄναλκι) too will cease (παύω, fut. mid.), and besides these the dishonour (ἀτιμία); just as the most wise Paul said also in the former letter; and we have been shown (ἀποδείκνυμι, pf. pass.) heirs (κληρονόμος) and sharers (μέτοχος) of the very kingdom (βασιλεία) of the saints; for he will say to us himself at the divine tribunal (βῆμα), the one in whom the yes: 'Come, the blessed (εὐλογέω, pf. ptc.) of my Father, inherit (κληρονομέω) the kingdom prepared (ἑτοιμάζω, pf. ptc.) for you from foundation (καταβολή) of world.' For household servants (οἰκέτης) we [are], as far as concerns the nature; but from slaves (δοῦλος) we were called (καλέω) into free (ἐλεύθερος) rank (ἀξίωμα) through him, from corruption into incorruption (ἀφθαρσία), from slaving (δουλεύω) to the devil (διάβολος) we were released (ἀπαλλάσσω, aor. pass.). Every promise [col. 324] of God therefore through Christ having the yes only (μόνον); wholly (παντελῶς) unacceptable (ἀπαράδεκτος) the no, which is the denial (ἄρνησις); for he himself is the truth. And he further shows (προσαποδείκνυμι) this one singly (ἑνικῶς), that by nature he is God; for if he would not belie (διαψεύδομαι) the promises, but rather will accomplish (ἀποπεραίνω, fut.) them for the saints, although it is the God and Father distributing (διανέμω) the goods, how would he not be Son by nature and truly, and as God from God, the one in whom 'every good giving (δόσις) and every perfect gift (δώρημα)' not falsely (διεψευσμένως)? That the word is without lie he further fixes (προσεμπεδόω) saying 'Therefore also through him to God the amen unto glory through us'; for since he himself is the mediator (μεσίτης), through whom also alone the Father [is] approachable (προσιτός), in whom every spiritual giving, through him surely also every end (πέρας) of prayer (εὐχή) will be; and this is the amen; and toward this the Son himself has trained (παιδαγωγέω, pf.) us, saying to the holy apostles: 'And in that day you will ask (ἐρωτάω) me nothing; amen amen I say to you, if you ask (αἰτέω) the Father anything, he will give to you in my name (ὄνομα); until now you asked nothing in my name; ask and you will receive (λαμβάνω), so that your joy (χαρά) may be fulfilled (πληρόω, pf. ptc.).' Through him then the amen to God the Father unto [stray numeral 2 omitted] glory through us. For it is custom (ἔθος) for us to close (κατακλείω) the end of every prayer in name of the Christ. And that he himself would not lack (ἀμοιρέω, opt.) the being glorified (δοξολογέω) fittingly (πρέπω), we shall see through (διοράω) without effort (ἀκονιτί), the blessed Jacob prophesying (προφητεύω): 'Judah, may your brothers praise (αἰνέω) you'; for Christ sprang up (ἀναφύω) from the tribe (φυλή) of Judah according to flesh; and moreover (γεμήν) Isaiah the prophet saying 'I saw the Lord Sabaoth sitting on a throne (θρόνος) high and [col. 325] lifted up (ἐπαίρω, pf. pass.)', and the seraphim standing around (περιίστημι, pf.), calling him holy, and naming him Lord Sabaoth, and saying heaven and earth to be full (πλήρης) of his glory. And that he beheld (θεάομαι, pf.) the Son himself, the wise John will show, saying: 'These things Isaiah said because he saw the glory [cut off; the quotation continues in the next section]'
pass_b_english: …obscure, but rather simple and true, saying, “Our word to you was not yes and no” (2 Corinthians 1:18). That is, he was not at war with himself or sick with inconsistency, praising a thing at one time and blaming it at another, but he spoke the truth in his preaching. So “God is faithful” (2 Corinthians 1:18), that is, free of falsehood and true.

The learned men of the Greeks will hold differing opinions about the gods they believe in, saying both yes and no; for truth is not among them, but rather falsehood. That is why they are tossed about by differing opinions. But He who is truly and by nature the Son of God Almighty, how could He become yes and no? …

Necessarily, then, the Son who is from Him by nature, “who was proclaimed among you by us, by me and Silvanus and Timothy, was not yes and no” (2 Corinthians 1:19). For every word about Him spoken through the voice of those who spoke for God has proved true. And “as many as are the promises of God,” he says, “in Him is the Yes” (2 Corinthians 1:20); that is, in Him we have received from God the Father every bounty and every promise. And this is “in the Yes,” that is, in truth; for these things have come to their fulfillment through Christ. For “death has been swallowed up in victory” (1 Corinthians 15:54), the power of corruption has been overthrown, and weakness too will cease, and dishonor besides (1 Corinthians 15:43), just as the most wise Paul also said in his first letter.

We have also been declared heirs and sharers of the very kingdom of the saints. For He in whom is the Yes will Himself say to us at the divine judgment seat, “Come, you blessed of My Father, inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matthew 25:34). By nature we are servants; but through Him we have been called from slavery to the dignity of the free, from corruption to incorruption, and we have been set free from serving the devil.

Every promise of God through Christ, then, has the Yes alone; the No, which is denial, is altogether inadmissible, for He Himself is the Truth (John 14:6). From this he also shows, of this One in particular, that He is God by nature. For if He would not break the promises, but will rather bring them to fulfillment for the saints, though it is God the Father who distributes the good things, how could He not be Son by nature and in truth, and God from God, He in whom, without falsehood, is “every good gift and every perfect gift” (James 1:17)?

That the word is free of falsehood he confirms further, saying, “Therefore through Him also is the Amen to God, for glory through us” (2 Corinthians 1:20). For since He is the Mediator (1 Timothy 2:5), through whom alone the Father can be approached, and in whom is every spiritual gift, surely through Him every prayer will also reach its fulfillment; and this is the Amen. The Son Himself has taught us this, saying to the holy apostles, “In that day you will ask Me nothing. Truly, truly, I say to you, if you ask the Father anything, He will give it to you in My name. Until now you have asked nothing in My name; ask, and you will receive, that your joy may be full” (John 16:23–24). Through Him, then, is the Amen to God the Father, for glory through us. For it is our custom to close every prayer in the name of Christ.

That He Himself would not lack the glory that befits Him we shall see without effort, when the blessed Jacob prophesies, “Judah, may your brothers praise you” (Genesis 49:8), for Christ sprang from the tribe of Judah according to the flesh (Hebrews 7:14); and when the prophet Isaiah says, “I saw the Lord of hosts sitting on a throne, high and lifted up” (Isaiah 6:1), with the seraphim standing around Him, calling Him holy, naming Him Lord of hosts, and saying that heaven and earth are full of His glory (Isaiah 6:2–3). And that it was the Son Himself whom he beheld, the wise John will show when he says, “Isaiah said these things because he saw His glory …
